Module 0. Foundations refresher: R and regression

Answer key

source(here::here("R", "setup.R"))
walk_base <- load_walk("baseline")

This answer key works through every exercise in workbook/wb00-refresher.qmd with complete, executed code and model answers. Numbers in the written answers are produced by inline R, so they match the output exactly. Marking notes after each exercise describe acceptable alternatives and common errors.

WarningSimulated data

All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.

1 Guided exercises

1.1 Exercise 1. Project, data and first summaries (LO 0.1)

a.

here::here("data", "walk_baseline.csv")
#> [1] "C:/Users/hp/Documents/Neudata Consultancy/Workshops & Training/Longitudinal Data Analysis/data/walk_baseline.csv"

here() returns the full path to the file, built from the project root. The same code works on any computer and from any subfolder (scripts, notes, workbook), because it does not depend on the current working directory or on where the project folder sits. A typed absolute path works only on the computer and in the folder where it was written.

b.

walk_base <- walk_base |>
  mutate(
    age10  = (age - 60) / 10,
    bmi_c  = bmi - 29,
    hyp150 = as.integer(sbp0 >= 150)
  )

by_sex <- walk_base |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_sbp0 = mean(sbp0), sd_sbp0 = sd(sbp0),
            pct_150 = 100 * mean(hyp150))
by_sex
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   sex        n mean_sbp0 sd_sbp0 pct_150
#>   <fct>  <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Male     170     149.6   13.19      50
#> 2 Female   190     144.6   12.93      40

There are 170 men and 190 women. Mean baseline SBP is 149.6 mmHg in men and 144.6 mmHg in women; 50% of men and 40% of women have SBP of at least 150 mmHg.

c.

walk_base |>
  filter(arm == "EP") |>
  select(id, age, sex, bmi, sbp0) |>
  arrange(desc(sbp0)) |>
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   id      age sex      bmi  sbp0
#>   <chr> <dbl> <fct>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 W100     73 Male    27.5   188
#> 2 W189     80 Female  33.4   173
#> 3 W292     49 Male    35.5   173
#> 4 W298     56 Female  29.4   173
#> 5 W050     48 Male    30.2   171

d.

ggplot(walk_base, aes(sbp0)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#9A9A9A", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, labeller = as_labeller(walk_arm_labels)) +
  labs(x = "Baseline SBP (mmHg)", y = "Participants")

The three distributions have similar centre, spread and shape. This is expected because arm was randomised: at baseline, before any intervention, the arms differ only by chance.

Marking notes. Accept read_csv(here(...)) followed by manual factor conversion instead of load_walk(). A common error is filter(arm = "EP") (single equals sign), which gives an error; the comparison needs ==. Accept any sensible bin width.

1.2 Exercise 2. Linear regression and categorical predictors (LO 0.2)

a.

m_lin <- lm(sbp0 ~ age10 + sex + bmi_c, data = walk_base)
summary(m_lin)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = sbp0 ~ age10 + sex + bmi_c, data = walk_base)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
#> -30.77 -10.05   0.51   8.94  37.83 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  149.322      0.984  151.71  < 2e-16 ***
#> age10          1.372      0.757    1.81  0.07069 .  
#> sexFemale     -4.809      1.353   -3.55  0.00043 ***
#> bmi_c          0.625      0.160    3.90  0.00012 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 12.8 on 356 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.0816, Adjusted R-squared:  0.0738 
#> F-statistic: 10.5 on 3 and 356 DF,  p-value: 1.18e-06
ci <- confint(m_lin)
ci
#>                2.5 %   97.5 %
#> (Intercept) 147.3860 151.2574
#> age10        -0.1164   2.8607
#> sexFemale    -7.4703  -2.1476
#> bmi_c         0.3093   0.9397

b.

  • Intercept. The estimated mean baseline SBP for a 60-year-old man with BMI 29 kg/m² is 149.3 (147.4 to 151.3) mmHg.
  • age10. Among participants of the same sex and BMI, those 10 years older have mean SBP 1.4 mmHg higher (95% CI -0.1 to 2.9).
  • sexFemale. Women have mean SBP 4.8 mmHg lower than men of the same age and BMI (95% CI -7.5 to -2.1).
  • bmi_c. Each 1 kg/m² higher BMI is associated with 0.62 mmHg higher mean SBP among participants of the same age and sex (95% CI 0.31 to 0.94).

c. The p-value for age10 is 0.071. It says that an age coefficient at least this far from zero would occur in about 7% of studies if there were truly no association between age and SBP (given the other predictors). It does not say that there is no association: the confidence interval includes values up to 2.9 mmHg per decade. Nor does it give the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

d. R2R^2 = 0.082: the three predictors explain about 8% of the variance in baseline SBP. This does not make the BMI coefficient unreliable. Its precision depends on its standard error (here 0.16), which is small enough to give a fairly narrow interval. Low R2R^2 says only that most of the variation between people has other causes.

e.

m_clin <- lm(sbp0 ~ clinic, data = walk_base)
round(coef(m_clin), 2)
#> (Intercept)     clinic2     clinic3     clinic4     clinic5     clinic6 
#>      141.56        4.87        4.20        2.67        9.62        7.56 
#>     clinic7     clinic8 
#>        2.42       12.02
m_clin5 <- lm(sbp0 ~ relevel(clinic, ref = "5"), data = walk_base)
round(coef(m_clin5), 2)
#>                 (Intercept) relevel(clinic, ref = "5")1 
#>                      151.18                       -9.62 
#> relevel(clinic, ref = "5")2 relevel(clinic, ref = "5")3 
#>                       -4.76                       -5.42 
#> relevel(clinic, ref = "5")4 relevel(clinic, ref = "5")6 
#>                       -6.96                       -2.07 
#> relevel(clinic, ref = "5")7 relevel(clinic, ref = "5")8 
#>                       -7.20                        2.40
# fitted clinic means agree
all.equal(fitted(m_clin), fitted(m_clin5))
#> [1] TRUE

Clinic 1 is the reference (the first factor level). The intercept, 141.6 mmHg, is the mean baseline SBP in clinic 1, and the clinic8 coefficient, 12 mmHg, is the difference in mean baseline SBP between clinic 8 and clinic 1. With clinic 5 as reference, the coefficients change because they now compare each clinic with clinic 5, but the fitted values (the clinic means) are identical.

Marking notes. Full credit for interpretations that give units, the interval and the adjustment set. Deduct for “age has no effect” in part c. In part e, accept factor(clinic, levels = c(5, 1:4, 6:8)).

1.3 Exercise 3. A continuous-by-categorical interaction (LO 0.3)

a.

m_bmi_sex <- lm(sbp0 ~ bmi_c * sex + age10, data = walk_base)
summary(m_bmi_sex)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = sbp0 ~ bmi_c * sex + age10, data = walk_base)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
#> -31.58  -9.89   0.51   9.22  38.00 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)      149.245      0.989  150.89  < 2e-16 ***
#> bmi_c              0.770      0.238    3.24  0.00133 ** 
#> sexFemale         -4.733      1.357   -3.49  0.00055 ***
#> age10              1.470      0.766    1.92  0.05590 .  
#> bmi_c:sexFemale   -0.269      0.325   -0.83  0.40872    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 12.8 on 355 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.0833, Adjusted R-squared:  0.073 
#> F-statistic: 8.07 on 4 and 355 DF,  p-value: 3.1e-06
ci3 <- confint(m_bmi_sex)

b. With FiF_i the female indicator, the fitted mean is ŷ=149.24+0.77bmi_c−4.73F+1.47age10−0.269bmi_cF\hat y = 149.24 + 0.77\,\text{bmi\_c} -4.73\,F + 1.47\,\text{age10} -0.269\,\text{bmi\_c}\,F.

  • Men (F=0F = 0): mean =149.24+0.77bmi_c+1.47age10= 149.24 + 0.77\,\text{bmi\_c} + 1.47\,\text{age10}. BMI slope 0.77 mmHg per kg/m².
  • Women (F=1F = 1): mean =144.51+0.501bmi_c+1.47age10= 144.51 + 0.501\,\text{bmi\_c} + 1.47\,\text{age10}. BMI slope 0.501 mmHg per kg/m².

c. sexFemale = -4.73 mmHg is the difference in mean SBP between women and men at a BMI of 29 kg/m² (where bmi_c = 0) and the same age. At other BMIs the sex difference is different, because the slopes differ.

d. The interaction coefficient, -0.27 (-0.91 to 0.37) mmHg per kg/m², is the women’s BMI slope minus the men’s. The interval includes zero and p = 0.409, so there is no clear evidence that the BMI slope differs between men and women. The interval is wide, so moderate differences cannot be ruled out either.

e.

m_bmi_sex_raw <- lm(sbp0 ~ bmi * sex + age10, data = walk_base)
round(cbind(centred = coef(m_bmi_sex), uncentred = coef(m_bmi_sex_raw)), 3)
#>                 centred uncentred
#> (Intercept)     149.245   126.919
#> bmi_c             0.770     0.770
#> sexFemale        -4.733     3.069
#> age10             1.470     1.470
#> bmi_c:sexFemale  -0.269    -0.269

The BMI slope (in men), the age coefficient and the interaction are identical. The intercept and the sexFemale coefficient change: they now refer to BMI = 0, so sexFemale (3.1 mmHg) is the sex difference at an impossible BMI of zero. The fitted values are the same; only the meaning of the coefficients that are evaluated at “BMI = 0” moves.

f.

emtrends(m_bmi_sex, ~ sex, var = "bmi_c")
#>  sex    bmi_c.trend    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
#>  Male         0.770 0.238 355   0.3020    1.238
#>  Female       0.501 0.219 355   0.0696    0.932
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95

Marking notes. The key point is part c: “at BMI 29”. Deduct if the interaction is described as “the BMI slope in women”. Accept bmi_c + sex + bmi_c:sex in place of *.

1.4 Exercise 4. Residual checks (LO 0.4)

a.

diag_df <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_lin), resid = resid(m_lin),
                      std_resid = rstandard(m_lin))
p1 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = "Fitted SBP (mmHg)", y = "Residual (mmHg)")
p2 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(sample = std_resid)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.5) + stat_qq_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical normal quantile", y = "Standardised residual")
p1 + p2

b. The residual-versus-fitted plot checks the mean structure (a curve would mean a missing nonlinear term or interaction) and constant variance (a funnel would mean the variance changes with the mean). Here the residuals form an even band around zero; the smooth curve turns up only at the far left, where there are very few points. The Q–Q plot checks normality of the residuals. The points follow the line closely, with a mild departure at the lower end (the most negative residuals are a little less extreme than normal), which is unimportant with 360 participants.

c. Independence of the residuals. It is judged from the study design: here each participant contributes one row and participants were recruited separately, so independence is reasonable. (Clustering by clinic is a possible exception, which Module 13 considers.)

d.

set.seed(1)
y_het <- 100 + 2 * walk_base$bmi_c + rnorm(360, 0, 0.5 * (walk_base$bmi - 18))
m_het <- lm(y_het ~ bmi_c, data = walk_base)
ggplot(data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_het), resid = resid(m_het)),
       aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Fitted value", y = "Residual")

The residuals fan out as the fitted value increases (a funnel shape). This violates the constant-variance assumption. The coefficient estimate is still unbiased, but the usual standard errors are not quite right.

Marking notes. Accept base R plot(m_lin, which = 1:2). A common error is to say the Q–Q plot checks “normality of the outcome”: it checks the residuals.

1.5 Exercise 5. Logistic regression for dropout (LO 0.2)

a.

walk_base <- walk_base |> mutate(sbp0_10 = (sbp0 - 150) / 10)
m_drop <- glm(dropout ~ sbp0_10 + arm, family = binomial, data = walk_base)
summary(m_drop)
#> 
#> Call:
#> glm(formula = dropout ~ sbp0_10 + arm, family = binomial, data = walk_base)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)  -1.2681     0.2273   -5.58  2.4e-08 ***
#> sbp0_10       0.2469     0.1018    2.43    0.015 *  
#> armSP        -0.3118     0.3358   -0.93    0.353    
#> armEP         0.0639     0.3166    0.20    0.840    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
#> 
#>     Null deviance: 360.29  on 359  degrees of freedom
#> Residual deviance: 352.90  on 356  degrees of freedom
#> AIC: 360.9
#> 
#> Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4
or_drop <- exp(cbind(OR = coef(m_drop), confint(m_drop)))
#> Waiting for profiling to be done...
round(or_drop, 3)
#>                OR 2.5 % 97.5 %
#> (Intercept) 0.281 0.177  0.432
#> sbp0_10     1.280 1.051  1.568
#> armSP       0.732 0.376  1.410
#> armEP       1.066 0.572  1.990

b. Each 10 mmHg higher baseline SBP is associated with 1.28 times the odds of dropping out (95% CI 1.05 to 1.57, p = 0.015), within the same arm: about 28% higher odds per 10 mmHg.

c. Compared with usual care, the odds of dropout were 0.73 (0.38 to 1.41) in SP and 1.07 (0.57 to 1.99) in EP, for participants with the same baseline SBP. Both intervals are wide and include 1, so the data do not show a clear difference in dropout between arms.

d.

nd5 <- data.frame(sbp0_10 = c(-2, 2), arm = factor("UC", levels = c("UC", "SP", "EP")))
lp5 <- predict(m_drop, nd5, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
pr5 <- data.frame(sbp0 = c(130, 170), prob = plogis(lp5$fit),
                  lower = plogis(lp5$fit - 1.96 * lp5$se.fit),
                  upper = plogis(lp5$fit + 1.96 * lp5$se.fit))
round(pr5, 3)
#>   sbp0  prob lower upper
#> 1  130 0.147 0.088 0.234
#> 2  170 0.316 0.199 0.461

For a usual-care participant with baseline SBP 130 mmHg, the estimated probability of dropout is 0.15 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.23); with 170 mmHg it is 0.32 (0.2 to 0.46).

e. If people with higher SBP are more likely to leave, the people still observed at month 12 have lower SBP on average than the full randomised group would have had. A simple average of the observed month-12 values would then be biased downwards. Methods that use all the earlier measurements, such as mixed models under a missing-at-random assumption, can correct for this (Modules 2 and 10).

Marking notes. Accept Wald intervals (confint.default). Common errors: interpreting the coefficient per 1 mmHg after rescaling; building the probability interval as prob ± 1.96 × SE.

1.6 Exercise 6. Confidence and prediction intervals (LO 0.5)

a.

new_women <- data.frame(age10 = 1, bmi_c = c(0, 6),
                        sex = factor("Female", levels = c("Male", "Female")))
ci6 <- predict(m_lin, new_women, interval = "confidence")
pi6 <- predict(m_lin, new_women, interval = "prediction")
round(cbind(bmi = c(29, 35), ci6, pi6[, -1]), 1)
#>   bmi   fit   lwr   upr   lwr   upr
#> 1  29 145.9 143.6 148.2 120.7 171.1
#> 2  35 149.6 146.6 152.6 124.3 174.9

b. For 70-year-old women with BMI 35 kg/m², the average SBP is estimated to be 149.6 mmHg, and we are 95% confident that the true average lies between 146.6 and 152.6 mmHg. An individual new woman of this kind could plausibly have SBP anywhere between about 124 and 175 mmHg, because individuals vary a great deal around the average.

c. The confidence interval would shrink, roughly by a factor of 10≈3.2\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2, because it reflects only uncertainty about the coefficients. The prediction interval would barely change: it is dominated by the residual SD (σ̂\hat\sigma = 12.8 mmHg), which is a property of the population, not of the sample size.

d.

grid6 <- data.frame(age10 = 1, sex = factor("Female", levels = c("Male", "Female")),
                    bmi_c = seq(19, 40, by = 0.5) - 29)
b6 <- cbind(grid6, as.data.frame(predict(m_lin, grid6, interval = "confidence")),
            setNames(as.data.frame(predict(m_lin, grid6, interval = "prediction"))[, 2:3],
                     c("plo", "phi"))) |>
  mutate(bmi = bmi_c + 29)
ggplot(b6, aes(bmi)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = plo, ymax = phi), fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = "#D55E00") +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m²)", y = "SBP (mmHg)")

Marking notes. age10 = 1 corresponds to age 70. A common error is age10 = 70. The key conceptual point in part c is that the prediction interval does not shrink to zero.

2 Independent exercises

2.1 Exercise 7. Daily steps and blood pressure (LO 0.2, 0.4)

walk_base <- walk_base |> mutate(steps_c = steps0 - 6)
m_steps <- lm(sbp0 ~ steps_c + age10 + sex + bmi_c, data = walk_base)
summary(m_steps)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = sbp0 ~ steps_c + age10 + sex + bmi_c, data = walk_base)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
#> -30.47 -10.08  -0.17   8.58  34.31 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  149.165      0.970  153.77  < 2e-16 ***
#> steps_c       -1.044      0.298   -3.50  0.00052 ***
#> age10          1.446      0.745    1.94  0.05325 .  
#> sexFemale     -4.500      1.335   -3.37  0.00083 ***
#> bmi_c          0.529      0.160    3.31  0.00104 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 12.6 on 355 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.112,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.102 
#> F-statistic: 11.2 on 4 and 355 DF,  p-value: 1.4e-08
ci7 <- confint(m_steps)
d7 <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_steps), resid = resid(m_steps),
                 std_resid = rstandard(m_steps))
(ggplot(d7, aes(fitted, resid)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#0072B2") +
    labs(x = "Fitted SBP (mmHg)", y = "Residual (mmHg)")) +
  (ggplot(d7, aes(sample = std_resid)) + stat_qq(alpha = 0.5) +
     stat_qq_line(colour = "#0072B2") +
     labs(x = "Theoretical normal quantile", y = "Standardised residual"))

Model answer. We regressed baseline SBP on baseline daily steps (centred at 6,000/day), age (per 10 years, centred at 60), sex and BMI (centred at 29 kg/m²). Each additional 1,000 steps per day was associated with -1.04 (-1.63 to -0.46) mmHg difference in mean SBP (p < 0.001), among participants of the same age, sex and BMI. The model explained 11.2% of the variance (residual SD 12.6 mmHg). Residual plots showed no important departures from linearity, constant variance or normality. The true between-person association of −1.5 mmHg per 1,000 steps/day, known only because the data are simulated, lies inside the 95% confidence interval.

Marking notes. Students should note that this is a between-person, observational association and could be confounded by unmeasured factors. Accept uncentred steps if the intercept is not interpreted.

2.2 Exercise 8. Does the steps association differ by sex? (LO 0.3)

m_steps_sex <- lm(sbp0 ~ steps_c * sex + age10 + bmi_c, data = walk_base)
summary(m_steps_sex)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = sbp0 ~ steps_c * sex + age10 + bmi_c, data = walk_base)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
#> -30.61  -9.81  -0.02   8.70  34.35 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                   Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)        149.120      0.973  153.21  < 2e-16 ***
#> steps_c             -1.246      0.431   -2.89  0.00406 ** 
#> sexFemale           -4.481      1.337   -3.35  0.00089 ***
#> age10                1.428      0.747    1.91  0.05666 .  
#> bmi_c                0.534      0.160    3.33  0.00096 ***
#> steps_c:sexFemale    0.383      0.590    0.65  0.51710    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 12.6 on 354 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.113,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.101 
#> F-statistic: 9.04 on 5 and 354 DF,  p-value: 4.18e-08
ci8 <- confint(m_steps_sex)
emtrends(m_steps_sex, ~ sex, var = "steps_c")
#>  sex    steps_c.trend    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
#>  Male          -1.246 0.431 354    -2.09  -0.3985
#>  Female        -0.863 0.409 354    -1.67  -0.0583
#> 
#> Confidence level used: 0.95

Model answer. The intercept (149.1 mmHg) is the mean SBP for a 60-year-old man with BMI 29 who walks 6,000 steps per day. The steps_c main effect (-1.25 mmHg per 1,000 steps/day) is now the steps slope in men. The sexFemale coefficient (-4.48 mmHg) is the sex difference at 6,000 steps per day. The interaction, 0.38 (-0.78 to 1.54) mmHg per 1,000 steps/day (p = 0.517), is the difference between the women’s and men’s steps slopes; the women’s slope is -0.86. The interval includes zero, so there is no clear evidence that the association differs by sex. Age and BMI keep their usual interpretations.

2.3 Exercise 9. Steps and the odds of SBP ≥ 150 (LO 0.2, 0.5)

m_hyp_steps <- glm(hyp150 ~ steps_c + age10 + sex + bmi_c, family = binomial,
                   data = walk_base)
or9 <- exp(cbind(OR = coef(m_hyp_steps), confint(m_hyp_steps)))
#> Waiting for profiling to be done...
round(or9, 3)
#>                OR 2.5 % 97.5 %
#> (Intercept) 0.956 0.702  1.300
#> steps_c     0.899 0.814  0.989
#> age10       1.221 0.962  1.556
#> sexFemale   0.686 0.447  1.052
#> bmi_c       1.060 1.006  1.117
nd9 <- data.frame(steps_c = c(-2, 4), age10 = 0, bmi_c = 0,
                  sex = factor("Female", levels = c("Male", "Female")))
lp9 <- predict(m_hyp_steps, nd9, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
pr9 <- data.frame(steps = c(4000, 10000), prob = plogis(lp9$fit),
                  lower = plogis(lp9$fit - 1.96 * lp9$se.fit),
                  upper = plogis(lp9$fit + 1.96 * lp9$se.fit))
round(pr9, 3)
#>   steps  prob lower upper
#> 1  4000 0.448 0.363 0.537
#> 2 10000 0.300 0.208 0.410

Model answer. Each additional 1,000 steps per day was associated with an odds ratio of 0.899 (0.814 to 0.989) for baseline SBP ≥ 150 mmHg, adjusted for age, sex and BMI. For a 60-year-old woman with BMI 29, the estimated probability is 0.45 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.54) at 4,000 steps/day and 0.3 (0.21 to 0.41) at 10,000 steps/day. These are estimated proportions among women with those characteristics. They do not say what would happen to an individual woman if she increased her walking: the association is between people and could reflect confounding. The interval at 10,000 steps is wider because few participants walk that much.

2.4 Exercise 10. A first look at repeated measurements

walk <- load_walk()
s_once <- coef(summary(lm(sbp0 ~ sex, data = walk_base)))["sexFemale", 1:2]
s_all  <- coef(summary(lm(sbp ~ sex, data = walk)))["sexFemale", 1:2]
rbind(baseline_only = s_once, all_visits = s_all) |> round(3)
#>               Estimate Std. Error
#> baseline_only   -4.985      1.378
#> all_visits      -3.538      0.619

Model answer. The baseline-only model estimates a sex difference of -4.98 mmHg with SE 1.38; the all-visits model gives -3.54 mmHg with SE 0.62. (The estimates differ partly because the follow-up visits include the effects of the programmes and the effects of dropout.) The all-visits SE is much smaller because lm() treats the 1897 rows as independent observations. But sex is a between-person characteristic: there are still only 360 people to compare, and repeated SBP measurements on the same person are strongly correlated. The all-visits standard error is therefore too small, and its confidence interval too narrow. Module 1 shows by simulation that this direction of error is general for between-person comparisons.

Marking notes. Full credit requires the direction (too small) and the reason (correlated measurements within person; information comes from the number of people).
